title: TB2-02732
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX and the person whom she alleges is her son, XXXX XXXX XXXX, the minor claimant, are citizens of Afghanistan. They claim protection under Sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS (From PIF Narrative of adult claimant (the "claimant" herein unless otherwise indicated) in Exhibit C-1):

The claimant is from Kabul. She was a XXXX, and her husband worked XXXX XXXX XXXX projects. On XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, 2011 her husband received threatening phone calls from the local well-known Taliban Commander XXXX to leave their jobs with the puppet government.

On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011 they moved and her husband spoke to a smuggler about coming to Canada. In XXXX 2012, he went to visit his brothers to get more money from land sales, but he never came back. She believes he was taken by Commander XXXX. She went to the police in Kabul but they said to report to XXXX province, but she did not because they were scheduled to leave.

The Panel finds the claimants not to be Convention refugees under Section 96,2 as they do not have a well-founded fear of persecution in Afghanistan on any of the five Convention grounds. The Panel also finds that the claimants are not persons in need of protection under section 97,3 as, on a balance of probabilities, their removal to Afghanistan would not subject them personally to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture. The Panel's reasons are as follows. The Hearing / Nature of Claim
The claimant gave the great majority of the oral testimony. Counsel questioned the minor claimant at the end of the hearing.

The Panel considered the issues of identity, credibility and the well-foundedness of the claimants' alleged fear of persecution, risk to life, etc., i.e., objective basis. The Panel considered all the evidence as well as counsel's oral submission at the close of the hearing. Identity

There was a problem in this area. The Panel accepts that the claimants are citizens of Afghanistan, from the copies of their Afghani passports supplied. However, the claimant could not establish that her alleged husband (her "husband") is in fact the father of the minor. Their mutual husband / father's name was not listed on their passports. On the taskera (National ID document) of the claimant, her husband's name is not mentioned. It is mentioned on the minor's taskera, though. Given the other credibility concerns herein, the Panel does not necessarily accept that the claimant was married to her alleged husband, nor that the claimants are indeed mother and son. The claimant could supply no marriage certificate nor birth certificate for the minor. The names of the claimant and the minor are in no part similar to each other. The claimant was asked how old she was when she gave birth to her son, and she said she was 37-38. However, as per the respective birthdates, the claimant would have been almost exactly 40, plus three days, when she gave birth to the minor. All the factors lead the Panel to find that the claimants are not mother and son. The Panel notes at this time that neither counsel nor claimant requested time, post-hearing, to provide further documents, missing as of the hearing, which might have assisted their claim. Credibility

The claimant could not document any part of their alleged route to Canada, nor that they were even in Afghanistan at any time after XXXX 2011. The alleged key events occurred later in 2011. The claimants did not make their refugee claims at the airport in Canada, so it is impossible to document when they arrived. Thus, it is possible the claimants were somewhere else than Afghanistan later in 2011. Thus, the Panel may have been deprived of the ability to conduct a full analysis of issues such as failure to, and previous claim, elsewhere, and delay in claiming in Canada.

The claimant alleged that she was a XXXX in Afghanistan. In fact, this is a significant part of her claim. To document this allegation, she presented Exhibit C-7, which purports to confirm she was a XXXX. She was asked why the document, allegedly issued by the Afghani Ministry XXXX XXXX XXXX, was in English. The claimant indicated that the document actually was issued in an Afghani language, but she, or her translator, substituted English for the Afghani language text. This was not noted on the document itself nor anywhere else in the file. The original document was not presented. Thus, the claimant admitted that she, or those for whom she is responsible, tampered with an alleged Government document, and presented it to the Board with no explanation or notation that this had been done. The Panel thus finds this document to be not genuine, in fact this has been admitted by the claimant. From this finding flows several other findings. From the submission of a false document the panel is entitled to make a general negative inference as to credibility, and it does so. Next, this document is afforded no weight in establishing that the claimant was a XXXX. As there was no other document supplied in this regard, the Panel finds that she was not a XXXX as alleged.

Another key allegation of the claimant related to her husband's employment. Both in the PIF Narrative and Exhibit R/A-2 the claimant alleged that her husband was a laborer. However, the job letter in Exhibit C-11 indicates that he was a XXXX XXXX XXXX which the Panel finds to be quite different from XXXX. When asked to explain the inconsistency, she said he was both a XXXX and XXXX XXXX, which does not explain the inconsistency, as it adds yet a third version of her alleged husband's alleged occupation. From this the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility, and further affords the job letter little weight, and thus finds that the claimant was not employed by the "XXXX" as alleged.

The claimant alleges that she was threatened by Taliban Commander XXXX, thus she had to leave Afghanistan. However, she could in no way document that this man exists, or existed, or had the alleged role in the Taliban. The only corroboration she could present were the "night letters" in Exhibit C-8. However, neither of these is signed by, or mentions, this man. With respect to these letters, the claimant did not complain to the police about them, thus further corroboration that these letters were received could not be supplied by way of police report. The claimant was asked why she did not mention the night letters allegedly received in her Narrative, since she knew about them at the time, and she said it was because the letters were at the time not in her possession. However, the Panel finds, this is not sufficient reason to omit from the PIF a very serious allegation, and from this omission the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility. Further, the claimant testified that in fact her husband did report the night letters to the police, when she had not mentioned this in her Narrative, and of course there is no police report.

The claimant was asked what this man said in the three alleged threat phone calls, and she said he threatened her and her husband to quit their jobs, or they would kill the minor. When asked if he said anything else, she said no. However, she was asked why she failed to testify as to what she had written in her Narrative, that he had also threatened to kill the claimant and her husband. She said she might have missed that. However, the Panel does not accept this explanation, considering the other credibility concerns herein, and from this omission the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

One of the night letters referred to not sending girls to school, and the claimant was asked why she would be sent such a letter, as she had no daughters. She said the letter was not addressed to her. When asked, why, then, she presented the letter, she said it was because the Taliban knows that, XXXX XXXX XXXX, she is in touch with other mothers who send their children to school. However, as the Panel has found that the claimant was not a XXXX, the Panel does not accept this explanation. As a result of all the above, and considering the other credibility concerns herein, the Panel finds that the night letters are not genuine, and that the three alleged threat calls did not actually occur.

The claimant testified that she quit her job as a XXXX as a result of the threats, and she said she did so in XXXX 2011. She was asked why she had indicated in her PIF that she left her job in XXXX 2011, and she said that she must have been confused, as she moved in XXXX 2011. Then she said she left her job in XXXX 2011. It was asked of her that since she alleged that the first threat call was on XXXX XXXX, 2011, why would she have quit earlier, in XXXX or XXXX 2011? Her answer was that she was not familiar with dates. However, the claimant used only the Canadian calendar in her Narrative, and did not allege conversion problems with the Afghani calendar. Thus, the Panel does not accept the claimant's explanations for these inconsistencies, from which the panel makes negative inferences as to credibility.

The Panel also does not accept that the claimant's husband was kidnapped as alleged. She says she went to the Kabul police to report it, who told her to go to the XXXX police to report it, but she did not. As a result, there is no police report, missing person's report, media article, etc., or anything else, to document this man's alleged kidnapping.

As indicated above, from all the above credibility concerns, the Panel finds the claimant's evidence to be, overall, not credible, and thus insufficient to support her claim for refugee protection Well-Foundedness of the Claimants' Alleged Fear of Risk to Life, etc. / Objective Basis, Testimony of Minor

Counsel questioned the minor, relatively briefly. The minor said his father was kidnapped, and his mother is at risk for being a XXXX, therefore he is at risk. However, as these allegations have been thoroughly rejected above, the Panel does not accept this argument of the minor.

The minor said that he feared abduction and recruitment by the Taliban, as a 16 year old, especially since they are from XXXX, allegedly a Taliban stronghold, and that they are Pashtos, the same ethnicity as the Taliban. However, the minor first said he was 17, which is a concern to the Panel in regard to identity, discussed above. The minor said this was a "mistake", however, the Panel notes, a teenager would easily be expected to know at least how old he is. For this reason alone the Panel has doubts about the minor's credibility.

The claimant was asked why there was an allegation, only at the very end of the hearing, that there is a fear on behalf of the minor of forced recruitment by the Taliban, when this alleged head of fear was never mentioned before in any previous submission of either claimant? She could provide no explanation, thus the Panel finds even the addition of this alleged head of fear to be an embellishment at the hearing, from which the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

However, it is evident the claimant is female, and the Panel notes from the documentation before it that there may be some risk or vulnerability for females living in Afghanistan without the protection of male family members. As indicated above, for credibility concerns, the Panel cannot even accept that the claimant would be without a husband if she hypothetically returned to Afghanistan, thus the Panel finds that the claimant would not be subject to persecution for this reason.

The Panel has also considered the situation of women in general in Afghanistan. It is hypothetically possible that the Taliban could target any females in Afghanistan, for kidnapping or even for not dressing in a fully Islamic fashion. There was no allegation that this has happened in the past, nor any convincing evidence that the situation has deteriorated significantly since 2011 when the claimants left Afghanistan. However, no persuasive evidence or argument has been adduced, nor is the Panel aware of any, that would make the female claimant more of a hypothetical target of the Taliban or other such potential agents of persecution than any other female Afghans. There was not any allegation that the family is of particularly high profile that would attract the attention of the Taliban or others, and, it is recalled, the allegations that the claimant was a XXXX and her husband worked for "XXXX" were rejected. No evidence was submitted that the family publicly expressed any political opinion opposed to the Taliban, or for the West of the Government. It is hypothetically possible that the Taliban could target anyone in Afghanistan. However, no persuasive evidence or argument has been adduced, nor is the Panel aware of any, that would make either of the claimants more of a hypothetical target of the Taliban than any other Afghans. In this regard, it is conceivably possible that the minor could be kidnapped by the Taliban for the purpose of forced recruitment, but there is insufficient evidence to suggest that this is anything more that a mere possibility, and the Panel finds that there is not even a serious possibility that the minor would be persecuted for this or any other reason upon a hypothetical return to Afghanistan.

As a result of the above, the Panel finds the claimants to not be Convention refugees under s. 96 nor persons in need of protection under s. 97 of the IRPA. As such, for the reasons noted above, the claims are rejected with respect to all claimants. (signed) "M. Sterlin" M.
